[79] At the second sitting, the Member asked the Appellant if he tried to get copies of documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium, to which he responded that he had not because they gave him temporary documents.48 The Appellant's counsel also asked him if he received any documents stating that his claim was refused, to which the Appellant replied that he had received a document that he had given to his lawyer in Belgium. The Appellant's counsel asked whether, if he was given the time to do so, he could contact that lawyer and ask him to send the document, to which the Appellant responded that he could not because he did not know the lawyer well, he did not remember his name and he had different lawyers.49

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Afghanistan. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
DECISION
[2] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
BACKGROUND

[3] The Appellant's allegations are as follows. The Appellant fears the Taliban in Afghanistan due to his cousin, XXXX employment as an XXXX for the United States (US) military and his father's former position in the Afghan army. The Appellant left Afghanistan in 2009 due to threats by the Taliban and made a claim for asylum in Belgium. His asylum claim and appeal were refused. The Appellant also fears criminals in Belgium due to his brother, XXXX role as an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for the Belgium police. Some of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX on are also active in Afghanistan and associated with the Taliban. The Taliban sent threatening letters to the Appellant and his family in Afghanistan. The Taliban abducted the Appellant's father and killed XXXX father.
[4] The Appellant left Belgium for the US on XXXX XXXX, 2017. On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the Appellant entered Canada. He signed his Basis of Claim (BOC) form on May 8, 2017.

[5] The Appellant's refugee claim was heard on March 21, 2019 and May 7, 2019. The Minister filed a Notice to Intervene on the basis of credibility and exclusion pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention. On September 12, 2019, the RPD rejected the claim on the basis of credibility, the Appellant's stay in Belgium and his claim for refugee protection in Belgium. The Appellant submits that the RPD was procedurally unfair and erred in its credibility assessment.
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION (RAD)

[6] The RAD applies a standard of correctness for questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law. The RAD may defer to the RPD in assessing findings involving the credibility of oral testimony if it finds that it had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances.1 In this appeal, I find that the RPD did not have a meaningful advantage.
NEW EVIDENCE

[7] The Appellant submits the following items as new evidence:
a. XXXX affidavit;2
b. XXXX's wife's BOC narrative;3
c. Taliban letters;4
d. Photograph;5
e. Appellant's affidavit;6
f. Appellant's wife's identity documents;7
g. Appellant's cousin's statement;8 and
h. Article, "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX," June 8, 2011.9

[8] According to the law,10 I can only accept evidence that:
i. arose after the RPD decision; or
ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

[9] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.11
Part of XXXX affidavit is admitted as new evidence

[10] The Appellant submits that his and XXXX affidavits were not reasonably available at the time of the rejection because they postdate the decision and they respond to issues raised in the RPD's decision which he could not reasonably anticipate.

[11] The Appellant submits that XXXX affidavit is provided to give information about XXXX refugee claim as he had been called to be a witness for the Appellant but was unable to attend the hearing. The Appellant submits that, upon review of the decision, it was clear that the RPD relied on XXXX refugee claim documents to its error, so XXXX affidavit is provided to clarify this issue. XXXX affidavit refers to the following: the close relationship between XXXX and the Appellant, the date that XXXX began working as an XXXX for the US military in Afghanistan, his family being threatened due to his work, his father being killed in 2011, his refugee hearing proceeding on the basis of his wife's BOC narrative because it was more accurate regarding dates and versions of events in Afghanistan than XXXX own narrative, XXXX not being able to attend the Appellant's hearing, the number of letters received from the Taliban, that the Appellant has difficulty remembering details when he is under stress, and that family members have advised him that the Taliban continue to look for XXXX and the Appellant.

[12] Paragraph 12 of XXXX affidavit refers to the Taliban continuing to look for Ahmad and the Appellant. This paragraph meets the legislative requirements for new evidence as it arose after the RPD decision. Paragraph 12 is relevant as it indicates a continuing risk to the Appellant. As this is a sworn document, paragraph 12 meets the credibility threshold for purposes of admissibility. Therefore, paragraph 12 of XXXX affidavit is admitted into evidence.

[13] I find that the remainder of XXXX affidavit does not meet any of the legislative requirements for new evidence. I reject the Appellant's submission that XXXX affidavit responds to issues raised in the RPD's decision which he could not have reasonably anticipated prior to the RPD decision. Rather, I find that the information that XXXX refers to in his affidavit could have reasonably been anticipated by the Appellant prior to the RPD decision.

[14] The Appellant's claim was partly based on his risk in Afghanistan resulting from XXXX employment as an XXXX for the US military. As such, XXXX BOC form was an exhibit in the Appellant's refugee claim.12 There are inconsistencies between the BOC narratives of XXXX and the Appellant which are significant and readily apparent from a review of the narratives. While XXXX narrative states he worked as an interpreter for the US military from 2012 to 2015, the Appellant's narrative states XXXX worked as an XXXX for the US military from 2009 to 2011. Further, while XXXX narrative states his own father disappeared in 2015, the Appellant's narrative states that XXXX father was killed in 2011. As a result of these inconsistencies being readily apparent from a review of the narratives, both of which were before the RPD, I find that these issues could reasonably have been anticipated by the Appellant prior to the RPD decision. I also note that the Minister's Counsel specifically raised the inconsistency regarding when XXXX worked as an XXXX for the US army at the hearing on May 7, 201913 and that the RPD decision was not made until September 12, 2019, four months after the date of the last sitting.

[15] As a result of the foregoing, I find that, aside from paragraph 12, the Appellant could reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to provide XXXX affidavit to the RPD before the decision. Aside from paragraph 12, XXXX affidavit does not meet the legislative requirements for new evidence and is not admitted into evidence.
XXXX wife's BOC narrative is rejected

[16] The BOC narrative of XXXX's wife, which was submitted as an exhibit to XXXX's affidavit, does not meet any of the legislative requirements for new evidence. I note that, aside from the Appellant's submissions regarding why XXXX affidavit is new evidence, the Appellant does not provide specific submissions explaining how XXXXs wife's BOC narrative meets the requirements for new evidence. As stated above, XXXXs affidavit states that he and his wife's refugee hearing proceeded on the basis of his wife's BOC narrative because it was more accurate regarding dates and versions of events in Afghanistan than XXXX's own narrative.

[17] I have considered whether XXXX wife's BOC narrative meets the requirements for new evidence as part of my independent assessment. XXXX wife's BOC narrative pre-dates the RPD decision. As outlined above, XXXX BOC narrative was before the RPD and the significant differences between the narratives of XXXX and the Appellant are readily apparent. Further, as noted above, the inconsistency regarding the dates that XXXX worked as an interpreter was specifically raised by Minister's counsel at the last sitting and the decision was made four months later. As a result of the foregoing, I find that the Appellant has not established that XXXX wife's BOC narrative was not reasonably available or that he could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring it to the RPD before the decision. I find that, in submitting XXXX wife's BOC narrative on appeal, the Appellant is trying to repair a deficient RPD record, which is not the purpose of new evidence on appeal. I note that I have no discretion to admit evidence submitted on appeal that does not meet the legislative requirements for new evidence.14

[18] As a result of the foregoing, XXXX wife's BOC narrative is not admitted into evidence.
The Taliban letters are not new evidence
[19] The Appellant submits five Taliban letters as an exhibit to XXXX affidavit.

[20] The Appellant's affidavit refers to the first Taliban letter not being submitted to the RPD as a result of his own oversight. He states that he thought that he had provided it to his lawyer at their meetings.15 The first Taliban letter is dated XXXX 2011.16 It predates the RPD decision. I find that the Appellant's explanation fails to reasonably explain why he did not provide this letter to the RPD before the decision. This is a significant document, and it is the Appellant's responsibility to put forth his best case at the RPD. I find that the Appellant is trying to repair a deficient RPD record, which is not the purpose of new evidence on appeal. As a result, I find the XXXX 2011 Taliban letter does not meet any of the legislative requirements for new evidence.
[21] The XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, XXXX XXXX, 2016 and XXXX XXXX, 2017 Taliban letters are not new evidence as they already form part of the RPD record.17

[22] The XXXX 2019 Taliban letter predates the RPD decision.18 The Appellant does not explain why it was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision or why he could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring it to the RPD before the decision. As a result, I find that the XXXX 2019 Taliban letter does not meet any of the legislative requirements for new evidence. It is not admitted into evidence.
The photograph is not new evidence

[23] The photograph submitted as an exhibit to XXXX affidavit is not new evidence as it already forms part of the RPD record.19
Some of the Appellant's affidavit is admitted as new evidence

[24] As outlined above, the Appellant submits that his and XXXX affidavits were not reasonably available at the time of the rejection because they postdate the decision and they respond to issues raised by the RPD's decision which could not have reasonably been anticipated by the Appellant. The Appellant submits that his own affidavit clarifies some of the errors of fact that were made by the RPD at the hearing and that these errors could not reasonably have been anticipated. The Appellant submits that his affidavit also provides new information regarding events in Afghanistan since the hearing regarding the Taliban continuing to search for him.

[25] Paragraph 25 of the Appellant's affidavit refers to the Taliban continuing to look for XXXX and the Appellant. Paragraph 25 is new as it arose after the RPD decision. This evidence is relevant as it indicates continuing risk to the Appellant. As the Appellant has sworn to its truthfulness, it meets the credibility threshold for purposes of admissibility. Therefore, paragraph 25 of the Appellant's affidavit is admitted into evidence.

[26] The Appellant's affidavit repeats much of the content already found in his BOC narrative and oral testimony including his risk in Afghanistan and Belgium, the Taliban threat letters, his father's abduction, his travel to the US and Canada and the circumstances under which he completed his original BOC form. The Appellant's affidavit also outlines alleged misunderstandings by the RPD that he states he did not realize until he read the RPD's reasons. I turn to these now.
The Appellant's evidence regarding the interpreter in Belgium is admitted into evidence

[27] Paragraph 24(a) of the Appellant's affidavit20 states that the RPD member did not ask him why he could not request another interpreter when he made his asylum claim in Belgium and that, if he had asked, the Appellant would have stated that he did request another interpreter and was told that no others were available. The Appellant submits that this explains why he followed his brother's instructions to tell Belgian immigration authorities that his whole family was dead, which was untrue.

[28] I have reviewed the transcripts of the hearing and agree that the Appellant was not asked why he did not request another interpreter when he made his asylum claim in Belgium. As a result, I find that the Appellant has reasonably explained why he did not provide this information at the hearing or before the RPD decision. Therefore, paragraph 24(a) meets the legislative requirements for new evidence.

[29] I find that paragraph 24(a) meets the jurisprudential requirements. It is new in the sense that there is no other evidence on the record regarding this issue. It is relevant to the Appellant's reasons for lying to immigration authorities in Belgium and therefore his credibility. As it is contained in a sworn affidavit, I accept that it meets the credibility threshold for purposes of admissibility.

[30] As a result of the foregoing, paragraph 24(a) of the Appellant's affidavit is admitted into evidence.
The Appellant's submission regarding the dates that XXXX was an XXXX for the US military is not new evidence

[31] Paragraph 24(b) of the Appellant's affidavit21 states that the RPD member did not put to his attention the dates on the documents regarding XXXX XXXX with the US military, nor question whether XXXX had ever actually been in the US military.

[32] The content of paragraph 24(b) is submissions, not evidence. I will consider these submissions later in these reasons.
The Appellant's statement regarding his asylum documents from Belgium are not admitted

[33] Paragraph 24(c) of the Appellant's affidavit22 states that he made efforts to obtain documents from Afghanistan and Belgium and that his cousin's lawyer, Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and his former counsel had difficulty obtaining documents from Belgium. After my review of the transcripts of the hearing, I note that the Appellant was asked about efforts made to obtain documents related to his asylum claim in Belgium.23 I find that the Appellant is providing additional explanations for the questions that he was asked during the hearing. The Appellant does not explain why he did not provide this information at the hearing or before the decision was made, which was four months after the hearing. As a result, I find that paragraph 24(c) does not meet any of the legislative requirements for new evidence. Paragraph 24(c) is not admitted into evidence.
The Appellant's statement regarding XXXX is admitted into evidence

[34] Paragraph 24(d) of the Appellant's affidavit24 states that the RPD member did not ask the Appellant whether he tried to obtain a letter or affidavit from XXXX, the undercover police officer in Belgium, to confirm that he told him about the threat he received in Belgium. The Appellant states that, if he had been asked, he would have explained that XXXX was an undercover member of the federal police and would not be in a situation to provide a letter of support.

[35] I have reviewed the transcripts of the hearings and agree that the Appellant was not asked whether he tried to obtain a letter or affidavit from XXXX. As a result, I find that the Appellant has reasonably explained why he did not provide this information to the RPD at the hearing and prior to the decision. Therefore, paragraph 24(d) meets the legislative requirements for new evidence.

[36] I find that the Appellant's statement meets the jurisprudential requirements. It is new in the sense that there is no other evidence on the record regarding this issue. It is relevant to the RPD finding that the Appellant lacked corroborating evidence. As the statement is contained in a sworn affidavit, I accept that it meets the credibility threshold for purposes of admissibility.

[37] As a result of the foregoing, paragraph 24(d) of the Appellant's affidavit is admitted into evidence.
The Appellant's statement regarding documents to prove his father was in the Afghan army is admitted into evidence

[38] Paragraph 24(e) of the Appellant's affidavit25 states that the RPD failed to ask him about documents to prove that his father was in the Afghan army. The Appellant states that, if he had been asked, he would have stated that all such records were destroyed by the Taliban as a threat to his father when he was young.

[39] I have reviewed the transcripts of the hearings and agree that the Appellant was not asked why he did not provide documents to prove that his father was in the Afghan army. As a result, I find that the Appellant has reasonably explained why he did not provide this evidence to the RPD at the hearing and prior to the decision. Therefore, paragraph 24(e) meets the legislative requirements for new evidence.

[40] I find that paragraph 24(e) meets the jurisprudential requirements. It is new in the sense that there is no other evidence on the record regarding this issue. It is relevant to the RPD finding that the Appellant lacked corroborating evidence. As the statement is contained in a sworn affidavit, it meets the credibility threshold for purposes of admissibility.

[41] As a result of the foregoing, paragraph 24(e) of the Appellant's affidavit is admitted into evidence.
The Appellant's wife's documents are admitted into evidence
[42] The Appellant's affidavit states that his wife left Afghanistan and sought refuge in Tajikistan in or about XXXX 2019. He submits a copy of her identification from Tajikistan.
[43] The Appellant's wife's documents meet the legislative requirement for new evidence as they were issued after the RPD decision.

[44] The Appellant's wife's documents meet the jurisprudential requirements for new evidence. They are new in the sense that there are no similar documents contained in the record. Although they are not probative of the Appellant's wife's reasons for leaving Afghanistan, they are relevant as they indicate that she left Afghanistan. The Appellant's wife's documents are credible as they are issued by foreign governments. The Appellant's wife's documents are admitted into evidence.
The cousin's letter is admitted into evidence

[45] The Appellant's cousin's letter refers to the Taliban continuing to look for the Appellant. The cousin's letter meets the legislative requirements for new evidence as it post-dates the RPD decision and its content relates to events that occurred after the RPD decision.

[46] The cousin's letter also meets the jurisprudential requirements. The cousin's letter is new in that there is little other similar evidence in the record. The cousin's letter is relevant to ongoing risk to the Appellant. The cousin's letter meets the credibility threshold for purposes of admissibility. The cousin's letter is admitted into evidence.
The article is not admitted into evidence

[47] The article regarding the killing of the Taliban commander predates the RPD decision. The Appellant does not explain why the article was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD decision or why he could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring it to the RPD before the decision. As a result, I find that the article does not meet any of the legislative requirements for new evidence. It is not admitted into evidence.
ORAL HEARING

[48] The Appellant does not request an oral hearing.26 However, as I have admitted new evidence, I am obligated to consider whether one should be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Subsection 110(6) states that the RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.27 As the admissible new evidence would not justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim, no hearing can be held in accordance with subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
ANALYSIS

[49] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.28
The RPD erred in some of its findings but they are not determinative

[50] I agree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD member's suggestion that there were additional credibility concerns that would not be addressed in its reasons precludes the Appellant from addressing such concerns on appeal. My reasons focus on the credibility concerns that are addressed in the RPD reasons.

[51] I also agree with the Appellant's submissions that the discrepancies between the Appellant's original and amended BOC forms should not be relied upon to impugn the Appellant's credibility in light of the circumstances in which the Appellant completed his BOC form, namely in detention, without the assistance of counsel and arguably without proper interpretation. As a result, I set aside the RPD's findings based on omissions from the Appellant's original BOC form.

[52] I agree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD speculated that, when he made his asylum claim in Belgium, he could have avoided the interpreter that his brother warned him about by requesting a different one and therefore erred in drawing an adverse inference from him lying to Belgium immigration. I set this finding aside.

[53] I agree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD erred in drawing an adverse inference based on the Appellant misleading Canadian immigration authorities upon arrival. Although the Appellant provided false information in his initial interviews with CBSA regarding his identity, background and travel history, a few days later, in another interview with CBSA, he admitted that he had been untruthful because he was afraid that he would be deported if they knew his true identity. I accept the Appellant's explanation as reasonable in the circumstances and set aside this finding.

[54] I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in drawing an adverse inference from the Appellant's failure to provide documents regarding his father serving in the Afghan army as he was not asked why he did not provide such documents and provided a reasonable explanation on appeal. I set this finding aside.

[55] Although I agree with the RPD that the Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with the objective documentary evidence regarding his brother's sentence, I agree with the Appellant's submission that his belief in his brother's innocence and whether he was correct in stating that his brother's co-workers supported him is not material to the Appellant's refugee claim. I agree that this should not have been used to impugn his credibility and I set this finding aside.

[56] I agree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD speculated when it found it unlikely that the Appellant faced threats in Belgium due to his brother's activities. I also agree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD erred in finding the Appellant's testimony regarding the alleged threats from the smugglers in Belgium vague. I set these findings aside.

[57] The Appellant is a citizen of Afghanistan. In its reasons, the RPD states that it "will not be addressing the issue of exclusion" and that "the issue of exclusion will not be looked at."29 As a result, although the Appellant's risk in Belgium is relevant to why he left Belgium or does not want to return there, his risk in Belgium is not determinative. Therefore, these reasons focus on the Appellant's risk in Afghanistan. Although I have found that the RPD erred in some of its findings, I find that, as a result of significant credibility concerns related to his risk in Afghanistan, as outlined below, the Appellant has not established his claim on a balance of probabilities. I turn to these now.
The RPD was correct in finding that the significant discrepancies in the BOC narratives undermine the Appellant's credibility

[58] The RPD found that there were significant inconsistencies and omissions between the BOC narratives of the Appellant and XXXX, specifically related to when XXXX worked as an XXXX for the US military, whether XXXX father was killed or disappeared, including the date that this occurred, and whether the Appellant's father was abducted by the Taliban.

[59] The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from these discrepancies and speculated that XXXX evidence was to be preferred in light of the finding of the RPD in XXXX case that there were significant credibility concerns. The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to acknowledge that the dates put forward in the Appellant's case were consistent with his allegations and the corroborative evidence he had filed, apart from XXXX claim. The Appellant submits that his evidence was consistent and made sense.

[60] I reject the Appellant's submissions and find that the RPD did not err for the following reasons. I find the Appellant's submission that the RPD speculated that XXXX evidence was to be preferred over the Appellant's evidence to be without merit. Rather than preferring XXXX evidence over that of the Appellant, the RPD member found that the discrepancies in their narratives raised significant credibility concerns in the claim that was before him, namely that of the Appellant. While I agree that the dates put forward in the Appellant's narrative and testimony were consistent with the corroborative evidence apart from Ahmad's claim, the Appellant's claim was partly based on XXXX claim. XXXX narrative was in evidence before the RPD. I find that the RPD did not err in considering it. Contrary to the Appellant's submissions, the RPD was not required to consider the Appellant's claim in the absence of XXXX narrative.

[61] The RPD member's reference to significant credibility concerns in the reasons in XXXX claim indicates that the RPD member deciding XXXX's claim had credibility concerns regarding XXXX claim. The RPD member's finding that there were significant credibility concerns in XXXX claim does not remedy the significant discrepancies between the narratives of XXXX and the Appellant, nor does it bolster the credibility of the Appellant's claim. I find that the RPD did not err in finding that the significant credibility concerns between the narratives undermined the Appellant's credibility.

[62] I have reviewed the record, including the transcripts of the hearing, as part of my independent assessment, and agree with the RPD that there were significant inconsistencies between the narratives of the Appellant and XXXX that undermine the Appellant's credibility. While XXXX narrative states that he took the XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2012, started working as an XXXX in 2012 and that, until XXXX 2015, experienced no direct threats, the Appellant's narrative states that XXXX worked as a XXXX for the US military from 2009 to 2011 and that they received a threat letter from the Taliban in XXXX 2011 threatening XXXX for his work as a XXXX with the Americans. The Minister's counsel put the discrepancies in the evidence regarding the dates that XXXX worked as an XXXX for the US military to the Appellant at the hearing, to which he replied that he could not speak to the information contained in XXXX BOC narrative, but that he himself was threatened in 2009 and provided documents to show that.30

[63] As noted by the RPD member, there are additional discrepancies in the narratives. While XXXX narrative states that his mother and father disappeared sometime in 2015, the Appellant's narrative states that XXXX father was shot coming out of a mosque one day after the XXXX 2011 threat letter was received and fails to mention XXXX mother. Further, while the Appellant's narrative states that his father was abducted by the Taliban in XXXX 2017, XXXX narrative does not mention the abduction of the Appellant's father, XXXX uncle, despite this occurring six months prior to XXXX completing his BOC form.

[64] After my independent assessment, I agree with the RPD finding that there were significant discrepancies between the narratives of the Appellant and XXXX which were not reasonably explained and which undermine the credibility of the Appellant's allegations.
The RPD was correct in drawing an adverse inference from the inconsistency in the psychiatric report regarding the Appellant's father

[65] The RPD found that the psychiatric report submitted by the Appellant was inconsistent with his other evidence. The RPD accepted the diagnosis of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and adjustment disorder with depressed and anxious distress but noted that the doctors were not in a position to state the cause of the Appellant's symptoms. The RPD noted that, while the report states that the Appellant's brother is living in Belgium and his father continues to live in Kabul, the Appellant testified that his brother went to Tajikistan after he was released from jail and, more importantly, that his father had been abducted by the Taliban.

[66] The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to properly consider the medical evidence. The Appellant submits that it is an error for the RPD to discount the medical evidence in its entirety due to mistakes noted therein which do not have a bearing on the substantive merits of the claim. The Appellant submits that the medical reports are put forth to substantiate that the Appellant suffers from PTSD as a result of his experiences and that it is an error for the RPD to discount the reports without considering the medical diagnoses they contain and how they may have affected the Appellant's behaviour while detained and at the hearing.

[67] I reject the Appellant's submissions and find that the RPD did not err for the following reasons. Contrary to the Appellant's submissions, the RPD did not discount the medical evidence in its entirety. As noted above, the RPD accepted the psychiatrist's diagnosis.

[68] Further, I find that the mistakes in the medical report do have a bearing on the substantive merits of the claim. The medical report directly contradicts the Appellant's other evidence regarding his father. While the Appellant's BOC narrative and oral testimony indicate that his father was abducted by the Taliban, the medical report states that his father continues to live in Kabul. The Minister's Counsel asked the Appellant about this at the hearing, to which the Appellant responded that he told the psychiatrist that his father used to go to Kabul to visit them.31 Appellant's counsel also asked the Appellant whether he told the psychiatrist that his father was living in Kabul, to which he responded that he told the psychiatrist that his father had been abducted.32

[69] I find the Appellant's explanation not reasonable in the circumstances. The medical report clearly states that the Appellant's father continues to live in Kabul, which directly contradicts the Appellant's BOC narrative and oral testimony that his father had been abducted. The Appellant's BOC narrative indicates that his father was abducted by the Taliban in XXXX 2017.33 The medical report indicates that the psychiatric assessment was completed on XXXX XXXX, 2018.34 Therefore, according to the Appellant's evidence, at the time of the assessment, his father had already been abducted. The medical report indicates that the Appellant's first language is Dari, which he spoke with the interpreter at the assessment.35 Considering these circumstances, I do not accept that the psychiatrist made an error in the report. I find that the Appellant has not provided a reasonable explanation for the discrepancy in the evidence regarding his father.

[70] I accept that the medical report was provided to explain the Appellant's behaviour while detained and at the hearing. However, the inconsistency regarding the Appellant's father arises from information he provided at a psychiatric assessment and his amended BOC narrative, which was completed with counsel and not while the Appellant was detained. As a result, I find that there is a significant inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence regarding his father that was not reasonably explained. I agree with the drawing of an adverse inference.
The RPD was correct in drawing an adverse inference from the inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence regarding the number of Taliban threat letters

[71] The RPD found that there were discrepancies in the Appellant's evidence with respect to the number of letters that the Taliban left. The RPD states that the Appellant only filed one letter with the RPD.

[72] The Appellant submits that the RPD ignored and misconstrued the evidence. The Appellant submits that the RPD reasons are confusing and inaccurate regarding the Appellant's evidence with respect to the Taliban letters. The Appellant submits that the RPD erroneously states that only one letter was filed with the RPD. The Appellant submits that, prior to the May 7, 2019 hearing, counsel filed two additional letters which the RPD allowed and on which the Appellant was questioned.

[73] I agree with the Appellant's submission that the RPD erred in stating that only one Taliban letter was filed with the RPD. The RPD record indicates that one letter was submitted prior to the hearing.36 The RPD record indicates that two additional letters were submitted prior to the second sitting,37 the Consolidated List of Documents indicates that the letters were entered as an exhibit38 and the transcript indicates that the Member asked the Appellant questions about the letters.39 However, I find that nothing turns on this error.

[74] After my independent assessment of the evidence, I agree with the RPD finding that the Appellant's evidence was inconsistent regarding the number of Taliban letters that were received. I have reviewed the record, including the transcripts of the hearing, as part of my independent assessment. In an interview with a CBSA officer on May 8, 2017, the Appellant indicated that he only received one threat letter from the Taliban.40 I note that the Appellant had the assistance of a Dari interpreter at the interview.41 In his amended BOC narrative, the Appellant states that his family received a threat letter from the Taliban in XXXX 201142 and refers to receiving two additional letters threatening his family.43 I note that the XXXX 2011 threat letter was not submitted to the RPD. The other two threat letters were before the RPD. At the first sitting, the Appellant initially testified that he received four to five threat letters,44 then later confirmed that he had received five letters.45

[75] According to the evidence, the Appellant did not receive any additional Taliban letters from the date of his interview with CBSA to the date of the last sitting. Therefore, his evidence regarding the number of Taliban letters he received should have been consistent in his interview with CBSA, his amended BOC narrative and his testimony at the hearing. However, the Appellant's evidence regarding the number of threat letters received in his interview, amended BOC narrative and testimony were all different. I acknowledge that the Appellant was detained at the time of his interview with CBSA. However, even if I were to accept that the circumstances of his detention caused the Appellant to provide incorrect information regarding the number of letters received, the inconsistency between his amended BOC narrative and testimony remains. I accept the psychiatrist's diagnosis that the Appellant has PTSD and adjustment disorder with depressed and anxious distress, however, I fail to see, nor do the Appellant's submissions or psychotherapy reports explain, how this would impair his ability to indicate the correct number of threat letters received. As a result of the foregoing, I agree with the drawing of an adverse inference.
Adverse inference from lack of documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium
[76] The RPD drew an adverse inference from the Appellant failing to provide documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium.
[77] The Appellant submits that the RPD erred by expecting documentary evidence without valid reasons for doubting the Appellant's credibility.

[78] I reject the Appellant's submission and find that the RPD did not err for the following reasons. As outlined above, I find that the RPD had valid reasons for doubting the Appellant's credibility. Moreover, after conducting my independent assessment, I agree with the drawing of an adverse inference from the Appellant's failure to provide documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium. I have reviewed the transcripts of the hearing as part of my independent assessment. At the first sitting, the Appellant testified that he applied for asylum in Belgium in 2009, was denied and appealed in 2010, and appealed again in 2013.46 The RPD member asked the Appellant whether he had documents from his asylum claim or appeal in Belgium, to which he responded that he did not because he was in a hurry to leave Belgium. The RPD member asked the Appellant whether he had tried to obtain these documents since being in Canada, to which he responded that he had not because he was busy with his own problems and does not know how to ask.47

[79] At the second sitting, the Member asked the Appellant if he tried to get copies of documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium, to which he responded that he had not because they gave him temporary documents.48 The Appellant's counsel also asked him if he received any documents stating that his claim was refused, to which the Appellant replied that he had received a document that he had given to his lawyer in Belgium. The Appellant's counsel asked whether, if he was given the time to do so, he could contact that lawyer and ask him to send the document, to which the Appellant responded that he could not because he did not know the lawyer well, he did not remember his name and he had different lawyers.49

[80] Rule 11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules requires that claimants provide acceptable documents establishing elements of their claim or explain why they did not do so and what steps they took to obtain them.50 According to the Appellant, he had two hearings and an appeal regarding his asylum claim in Belgium. He testified that he was in a hurry to leave Belgium, was busy with other problems in Canada, had not made efforts to obtain the documents, did not know how to do so, and did not know the names of his lawyers. I find the Appellant's explanations for his failure to provide, and lack of effort to obtain, documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium not reasonable in the circumstances.

[81] As stated by the RPD, these documents would allow it to determine whether the Appellant was consistent in his account of the basis for his claims in Belgium and Canada. I agree with the following statement of the RPD member:
[T]he claimant's application for refugee protection in Belgium, the decision made by the Belgian authorities and his application to appeal and the decision on appeal are all important documents to the Board in deciding his fears in Afghanistan and the credibility of the claimant.51

[82] As a result of the foregoing, I agree with the drawing of an adverse inference with respect to the Appellant's credibility from his failure to provide, and lack of effort to obtain, documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium.
CONCLUSION

[83] Sworn testimony of a claimant is presumed to be true unless there are valid reasons to doubt it.52 Although I have found that the RPD erred in some of its findings, which I have set aside, significant credibility issues remain which go to the core of the claim. These include significant discrepancies contained in the BOC narratives of XXXX and the Appellant, the psychiatric report, and the Appellant's evidence regarding the number of Taliban letters received, in addition to the Appellant's failure to provide, and lack of effort to obtain, documents regarding his asylum claim in Belgium. As a result of these discrepancies, I find that the Appellant has failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations that form the basis of his claim.

[84] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
